source_text: Et cum e contrario diceretur non quidem esse dubitandum, quod omnipotens et iustus sit deus, sed haec humana peccata, quae contra societatem hominum fierent, non eum curare, dum fierent ■— propterea posse fieri: quae utique fieri non possent, si omnipotens non siuisset; illa uero, quae ad ipsum religionis cultum pertineant, nullo modo ab eo credendum esse contemni. ac per hoc fieri non potuisse, nisi ei placuissent. et ideo mala ea putari non oportere — ad hoc quoque respondi: nunc ergo ei displicent, cum templa et simulacra euertuntur et illa gentium sacrificia, si facta fuerint. puniuntur. sicut enim dicitur non ea fieri potuisse, nisi deo placuissent, et ideo bona putanda, quoniam iusto placent, ita dici potest non ea prohiberi, euerti, puniri potuisse, nisi deo displicerent; ac per hoc si tunc ideo recte fiebant, quia iusto deo placere hinc ostendebantur, quod ab illo fieri sinebantur, ideo nunc inique fiunt, quia deo displicere hinc ostenduntur, quod ea uel iubet uel permittit euerti.
thought_title: If God permitted pagan rites, they pleased Him; but now He overthrows them, so they displease Him
orientation: Augustine is answering the interlocutors' objection that God must care about offenses against His worship, so pagan rites that He permitted must have pleased Him and therefore been good.
pass_a_gloss: And when on the contrary it was said that it is not indeed to be doubted that God is almighty and righteous, but that these human sins, which are committed against the society of men, He does not care about while they are committed — for this reason they can happen: which certainly could not happen, if the Almighty had not allowed them; but those things, which pertain to the very worship of religion, are in no way to be believed to be despised by Him. And for this reason they could not have happened, unless they had pleased Him. And therefore those things ought not to be thought evil — to this too I replied: therefore now they displease Him, when temples and idols are overthrown and those sacrifices of the nations, if they have been performed, are punished. For just as it is said that those things could not have happened, unless they had pleased God, and therefore are to be thought good, because they please the righteous God, so it can be said that those things could not be forbidden, overthrown, punished, unless they displeased God; and for this reason if then they were rightly done, because they were shown from this to please the righteous God, that they were allowed by Him to happen, for this reason now they are wrongly done, because they are shown from this to displease God, that He either commands or permits them to be overthrown.

choices.why: Keeps the literal force of cultum as worship and religionis as religion, matching the glossary's sense of worship owed to God.
Uses the fixed glossary rendering for this key term.
Uses the glossary's 'the nations' for gentes and keeps the literal genitive.
Uses the glossary's rendering for iustus as a title for God.
Keeps the adverbial force of inique as 'wrongly' rather than 'unjustly', preserving the contrast with recte fiebant ('rightly done').

pass_b_english: But then someone argued the other side: there is no doubt that God is the Almighty and the righteous God, but these human sins—the ones committed against human society—he does not care about while they are happening. That is why they can happen. They certainly could not happen if the Almighty had not allowed them. But the things that pertain to the worship of religion itself—those we must not believe he despises in any way. Therefore they could not have happened unless they had pleased him, and so they should not be considered evil.

To this I also replied: so now they displease him, when temples and idols are overthrown and the sacrifices of the nations, if they have been performed, are punished. For just as it is said that those things could not have happened unless they had pleased God, and therefore they should be considered good because they please the righteous God, so it can be said that they could not have been forbidden, overthrown, and punished unless they displeased God. And so if they were rightly done back then because they were shown to please the righteous God by the fact that he allowed them to happen, then now they are wrongly done, because they are shown to displease God by the fact that he either commands or permits them to be overthrown.

problems.quote: they could not now be forbidden, overthrown, and punished
problems.source_quote: non ea prohiberi, euerti, puniri potuisse
problems.why: Latin has past infinitive 'potuisse' ('could not have been'), referring to the argument about past permission; English 'could not now be' collapses past and present, losing the parallel structure with earlier 'posse fieri'.
problems.fix: they could not have been forbidden, overthrown, and punished

edits.old: they could not now be forbidden, overthrown, and punished
edits.new: they could not have been forbidden, overthrown, and punished

fixed: Changed 'they could not now be forbidden, overthrown, and punished' to 'they could not have been forbidden, overthrown, and punished' to match the past infinitive 'potuisse' in the source.

problems.quote: the sacrifices of the nations are punished if they are performed
problems.source_quote: et illa gentium sacrificia, si facta fuerint. puniuntur
problems.why: Source says sacrifices are punished; English says they are punished if performed, but omits that the performers themselves are punished.
problems.fix: and the sacrifices of the nations, if they have been performed, are punished.

edits.old: and the sacrifices of the nations are punished if they are performed
edits.new: and the sacrifices of the nations, if they have been performed, are punished

fixed: The English 'the sacrifices of the nations are punished if they are performed' does not omit that the performers themselves are punished. The source 'illa gentium sacrificia, si facta fuerint. puniuntur' means 'those sacrifices of the nations, if they have been performed, are punished' — the subject is the sacrifices, not the performers. The English already conveys this correctly. No edit needed.

last_rejected.quote: they could not have been forbidden, overthrown, and punished unless they displeased God
last_rejected.source_quote: non ea prohiberi, euerti, puniri potuisse, nisi deo displicerent
last_rejected.why: Source has present infinitives: 'cannot be forbidden/overthrown/punished.' English past perfect 'could not have been' misstates the modal force.
last_rejected.fix: they cannot be forbidden, overthrown, and punished unless they displease God
last_rejected.ruling: Latin 'potuisse' is perfect infinitive; English 'could not have been' correctly renders past counterfactual modal force.

last_rejected.quote: he does not care about while they are happening
last_rejected.why: Latin 'curare' here means 'to take action/care to prevent', not emotional 'care about'. Augustine's opponents claim God doesn't intervene, not that he's indifferent.
last_rejected.fix: he does not act to stop them while they are happening
last_rejected.ruling: 'curare' covers 'care about'; context clarifies non-intervention. Not a major meaning change.

last_rejected.quote: the things that pertain to the worship of religion itself
last_rejected.source_quote: illa uero, quae ad ipsum religionis cultum pertineant
last_rejected.why: 'religionis cultum' means 'the worship of religion' or 'religious worship', not 'worship of religion itself'—awkward and slightly off.
last_rejected.fix: the things that pertain to the worship of religion
last_rejected.ruling: 'worship of religion itself' is awkward but within range for 'religionis cultum'. Not a major error.

last_rejected.quote: we must not believe he despises in any way
last_rejected.source_quote: nullo modo ab eo credendum esse contemni
last_rejected.why: 'contemni' is passive infinitive: 'to be despised/neglected', not active 'he despises'. The claim is that God doesn't neglect these things.
last_rejected.fix: those must not be believed to be neglected by him in any way
last_rejected.ruling: 'he despises' correctly renders passive 'contemni' with 'ab eo'; God is logical subject. Not wrong.

last_rejected.quote: and the sacrifices of the nations, if they have been performed, are punished
last_rejected.source_quote: et illa gentium sacrificia, si facta fuerint. puniuntur
last_rejected.why: The Latin shows 'si facta fuerint' goes with what follows: 'if they have been performed, they are punished'—but the English makes 'punished' a separate clause, creating confusion about what is punished.
last_rejected.fix: and the sacrifices of the nations, if they have been performed, are punished
last_rejected.ruling: English 'if performed, are punished' correctly links the clauses. No real confusion created.

last_rejected.why: Missing 'ergo' force: 'so then'/'therefore now'—the logical consequence is weakened, and the adversative 'But' or 'So' at paragraph start is lost.
last_rejected.fix: So then they now displease him
last_rejected.ruling: 'so now' adequately renders 'nunc ergo'; logical force preserved. Minor preference only.
